source.title: Bridging the VLM and mech interp communities for multimodal interpretability

record.tranche_reason: The post argues that the superposition account may be confused with mixed selectivity and that inspecting only maximally activating images can misrepresent neuron function. These are refinements of the claim, but the post does not report a direct test of polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The post cites findings from other work, which are not recorded as results here. Its own qualitative GPT-4o example concerns the accuracy of neuron-activation captions, not whether neurons have unrelated functions. No result directly measures polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: This is an opinion and synthesis post. It reports no measurement of whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how often they do, or why. The remarks bearing on V3 and V7 are the author's stated doubts: superposition is 'questionable to me' and may be 'confused in practice with mixed selectivity', and peak-activation images 'may not' capture neuron function. Neither remark is backed by the post's own results. The one cited example of magnitude-dependent encoding, the 'politics neuron', comes from Goh et al. 2021. This falls short of T5, which needs results or a specific worked-out argument. The record's 'tests/T5' is therefore downgraded.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The author finds it unclear whether neurons or SAE features are the better unit, and doubts that max-activating images capture neuron function. She suspects superposition is often confused with magnitude-based mixed selectivity, so SAEs may alleviate the latter. She proposes combining circuit, text-image and captioning methods, plus a gold-standard ViT interpretability dataset. These are stated as opinions, not findings.
record.recipe_differences: The post discusses interpretability methods and issues but does not reproduce or apply the original method to test the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The author says neuron interpretations may depend on examining activation intervals rather than only maxima; the reported GPT-4o captioning experience also varied across prompt and heatmap approaches, though results remained poor.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4o misdescribed the region highlighted in a neuron's max-activating heatmaps (said birds/rabbit/dog instead of tree branches) across prompt and masking variants; a commenter found Claude 3.5 got it right.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: VLM-based neuron captioning can misidentify the activated feature, depending on the captioning model.

record.problems: The post is selective and primarily presents opinions and synthesis. The relevant GPT-4o example is qualitative and anecdotal, with no reported sample size, controls, quantitative scoring, or uncertainty. Other empirical findings mentioned are attributed to cited work.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results from the post were omitted.

untested.parts: All; Goh et al.'s multimodal neurons are cited only.
All; superposition is questioned only as an opinion, with no capacity or sparsity test.
All; the post suggests captioning across activation intervals but runs no comparison.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts are given because the post presents no results of its own on any version. The V3 and V7 points are worth noting as open hypotheses, but without data they do not qualify as challenges or scope limits.

versions.untested_parts: The post cites the multimodal-neuron work but does not test neuron responses to unrelated image inputs.
No language-model neuron prevalence or layer comparison.
The post questions superposition as a mental model and distinguishes it from mixed selectivity, but does not measure feature capacity, sparsity, or causal effects of capacity pressure.
No test of initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
No comparison of architectures, activation functions, regularization, polysemanticity rates, or performance costs.
The post raises concerns about neuron representations but does not test whether canonical mixed-response neurons have a shared feature or related jobs.

The post argues that examining only peak-activation images may be insufficient and suggests examining activation intervals, but does not compare polysemanticity judgments across ranges or scoring methods.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.operation_detail: Interpreted heatmaps for maximally activating images of a neuron.

conditions.value: maximally activating images for a neuron; correct interpretation described as branches of trees in the background
the prompt and many variations, including aggressive prompting
methods including masking out inactive purple areas

rows.measure: Qualitative correctness of GPT-4o's neuron-activation interpretation
rows.value: The post reports that results remained similarly poor; example interpretations identified birds, a rabbit, and a dog rather than branches.
rows.note: This reports an author's qualitative experience with captioning neuron activations, not a measure of neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: The row measures whether GPT-4o correctly captions a neuron's activation heatmap, an autointerp tool-accuracy question, not neuron polysemanticity. It is a single anecdote with no sample size. A commenter reports Claude 3.5 described the same image correctly, so the failure is specific to GPT-4o. Linking it to no version is correct.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
